newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Credit Suisse sees 8-member 1999 EMU start.
newsitem.headline: Credit Suisse sees 8-member 1999 EMU start.

text.p: Credit Suisse said it expected European economic and monetary union (EMU) to start on time with at least eight members, but that Spain, Portugal and Italy would probably have to wait for a second round to enter.

"We assume...that EMU will start on January 1, 1999 with at least eight countries (Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Austria, Ireland and Finland). The southern axis is the main point of discussion," the domestic banking branch of Credit Suisse Group said in a research report.

Southern countries' strict convergence efforts have put Spain and Portugal in better position to hit the three percent budget deficit target in 1997 than Germany or France, but Italy will not get its shortfall below four percent, analyst Fritz Stahel wrote.
"So will Italy have to wait while both other southern countries take part from the start? Such a decision against EC founding member Italy would be too sensitive politically."
Fear of getting off to a poor start in the single currency project with a weak euro argues against a broad EMU, Credit Suisse said, adding Germany would lead resistance to this.

"The question remains how to make clear to Spain and Portugal that they as well as Italy have to wait a bit. In this more probable case, clear promises to join in the next round (for example in 2001) as well as financial commitments are imperative," it said.

EU members can be spared this decision if the economic recovery in continental Europe goes worse than expected, making it hardly likely that Germany and France could push their budget deficits under four percent of GDP.
"In this case, the criteria would have to be interpreted so generously that a weak euro would be automatic and postponing the start date would be the most obvious solution," it added.
Financial markets can hardly be expected to wait calmly for another 12 months for a final decision, given the fact that prospects for an EMU postponement have become a central issue.

"If the politicians could count on markets' accepting a short delay, they would probably choose this path. On the other hand, markets are wondering if this option can be chosen in a politically credible way," it said.

As soon as fears arise that a delay would ease southern countries' convergence efforts, big market movements are likely, it said. Germany in particular would benefit from capital outflows sparked by rising interest rates in peripheral markets.
The Swiss franc would also firm against southern currencies, but less so than the mark because German investors would reduce their franc holdings as their fear of the euro wanes.
The most dangerous thing for Switzerland would be creation of a broad EMU in 1999, which would fuel strong demand for Swiss francs as a safe haven currency and choke off Swiss growth.

In this case, Italian bonds offer the most potential to gain, with the spread of 200 basis points over German government bonds likely to melt to around 30 points, it said. Expectations of high euro interest rates would undermine mark bonds, it said.
